terroir.climate: Mild and dry, sheltered by the Hunsrück and its Soonwald ridge to the north and west, with a long, sunny autumn; rainfall is low, around 500 millimetres, and spring frost on the valley floor is the main hazard. The upper valley is cooler and later, the lower valley near Bingen warmer; Riesling ripens between Mosel and Rheingau dates.
terroir.soils: The most varied in Germany: Devonian slate and quartzite in the upper valley at Monzingen; volcanic porphyry and melaphyre around Schlossböckelheim, Niederhausen and Traisen; red sandstone, conglomerate and loess around Bad Kreuznach; loess, loam and gravel in the lower valley towards Bingen. Each gives a different Riesling, from the smoky, taut wines of the porphyry to the broader wines of the loam.
terroir.topography: A winding valley with steep, rocky south facing slopes on the outer bends and the Rotenfels, a red porphyry cliff above Traisen, as its landmark; side valleys such as Bockenau's hold cooler sites. Vineyards run from Martinstein in the upper valley some fifty kilometres to Bingen, and the single Bereich, Nahetal, covers all of it.
terroir.water: The Nahe, small and quick, with its tributaries the Glan, the Alsenz, the Ellerbach and the Gräfenbach; it moderates the air and lights the slopes. The Brücke vineyard sits on its bank at Oberhausen, catching the mists and frost that make Eiswein possible.

traps: The Nahe is not a Mosel tributary; it is the Rhine's, and its wines are fuller than the Saar's and leaner than the Rheingau's.
Oberhausen and Niederhausen are neighbours: the Brücke belongs to Oberhausen, the Hermannshöhle to Niederhausen.
Rüdesheimer Rosengarten is Nahe, not Rheingau.
Schlossböckelheimer Burgweg is a Grosslage; Schlossböckelheimer Kupfergrube is the single site.
Riesling is under a third of the Nahe's vines, not the majority; Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder and the Pinots together outnumber it.

wines.note: Dry, medium bodied, grapefruit, blackcurrant leaf and wet stone at 12 to 13 per cent; with grilled fish, pork, chicken and vegetable dishes.
From Hermannshöhle, Kupfergrube, Felsenberg, Halenberg or Felseneck: smoky, taut and long; decant a young one, serve it with turbot or veal.
Lightly sweet at 8 to 10 per cent, apple, peach and herbs with the valley's mineral tang; a Spätlese with pork and apple or spiced dishes.
Botrytis Auslese with a gold capsule from the porphyry sites, and Eiswein from the Brücke's frost: honeyed, piercing, long lived.
Dry Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris from the loess, round and nutty; the everyday white of the valley's inns.
A small crop of Pinot Noir, light, dry and cherried, served cool.

exam: Place the Pfalz on the map: eastern foot of the Haardt, north of Alsace, south of Rheinhessen, warm and dry.
Know the two Bereiche, Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstrasse and Südliche Weinstrasse, and which is warmer.
Name the Mittelhaardt villages, Forst, Deidesheim, Ruppertsberg and Wachenheim, and the Forst crus Kirchenstück, Jesuitengarten, Ungeheuer and Pechstein.
Explain the basalt at Forst and the 1828 Bavarian tax survey as the roots of the Pfalz hierarchy.
Describe Pfalz Riesling against Mosel Riesling: riper, fuller, dry, spicy, higher alcohol.
Know the grapes beyond Riesling: Dornfelder, the Pinot family, Scheurebe, Rieslaner and Gewürztraminer.
Hold the German ladder, Prädikat by must weight, trocken and feinherb, VDP and the 2021 origin pyramid.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Fuller and riper than on the Mosel, usually dry, with yellow stone fruit, a spicy, smoky edge on basalt and sandstone, and firm acidity that keeps the weight honest.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.styles: This deeply coloured 1955 Weinsberg crossing is the most planted red grape of the Pfalz: soft, dark-fruited reds from easy quaffers to oaked bottlings.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Spätburgunder from the limestone and red slate of the south, Schweigen and Birkweiler above all, gives some of Germany's most serious dry reds.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder makes dry, creamy, understated whites that suit oak and food, and the VDP admits it to Grosses Gewächs here.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grauburgunder gives rounder, pear and nut scented dry whites, fuller than the Grigio style of Italy.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Still widely planted for simple, soft, early drinking whites, often sold dry as Rivaner.

grapes.name: Scheurebe
grapes.styles: An aromatic Riesling crossing of grapefruit and blackcurrant leaf, made dry, as Kabinett or as a botrytis sweet wine.

grapes.name: Rieslaner
grapes.styles: A late ripening Silvaner and Riesling crossing with piercing acidity, kept here for taut Auslese and sweeter wines.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: A Pfalz tradition, with ancient Traminer vines surviving at Rhodt; made dry or off-dry and heavily scented.

law.classification: The Pfalz is one of Germany's thirteen Anbaugebiete, the regions a Qualitätswein or Prädikatswein must name on its label. German law ranks wine first by must weight at harvest, from Qualitätswein through the Prädikat rungs Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein and Trockenbeerenauslese, and that ladder says nothing about sweetness in the glass. The 2021 reform added an origin pyramid, Anbaugebiet, then Region (the old Bereich), then Ort, then Einzellage and the smaller Gewann, and it made Erstes Gewächs and Grosses Gewächs protected legal terms for dry single-site wines, with the whole pyramid binding in full from the 2026 vintage. The Pfalz has two Bereiche, Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstrasse in the north and Südliche Weinstrasse in the south. The VDP's private pyramid, Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage and Grosse Lage, sits alongside, and in the Pfalz its Grosses Gewächs is open to Riesling, Weissburgunder and Spätburgunder.
labels: The northern Bereich holding the classic Riesling villages.
The southern Bereich, warmer, with more Pinot varieties and Dornfelder.
The German Wine Road, opened in 1935, running the length of the region from Bockenheim to the gate at Schweigen.
Legally dry: residual sugar at most 4 grams per litre, or up to 9 where the acidity is within 2 grams of the sugar.
Off-dry; feinherb is a customary term rather than a legal one.
A dry wine from a top classified single site; the VDP marks its own with an eagle on the capsule.
A rosé made from one named grape variety, at Qualitätswein level or above.
Grower sparkling wine, traditional method, from the estate's own grapes.
Estate bottled from the estate's own vineyards.
Müller-Thurgau sold dry under its alternative name.
tiers: Wine without geographical indication, the floor of the ladder.
Pfälzer Landwein: the protected geographical indication level, dry or off-dry.
Quality wine from one Anbaugebiet, in this case the Pfalz, with an official test number; enrichment of the must is allowed.
Quality wine with a ripeness attribute, Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese, ranked by must weight at picking and never enriched.

Protected terms for dry wine of protected origin from a named single vineyard: the ordinance caps Erstes Gewächs at 60 hectolitres per hectare, 70 on steep slopes, and holds Grosses Gewächs to a lower cap, hand picking and a later release.
The association's top site class; its dry wine is Grosses Gewächs, in the Pfalz from Riesling, Weissburgunder or Spätburgunder, hand picked and cropped low.

made.viticulture: Most Pfalz vineyards are gentle enough to work by machine, so this is a region of wire trained vines on flat or sloping ground rather than stake trained cliffs, and the economics are kinder than on the Mosel. The dryness of the rain shadow makes drought and heat the hazards of a warm year, so growers watch canopy shading, pick earlier than their parents did and have been quick to plant Pinot varieties on the warmest ground. Harvest for dry Riesling runs through late September and October, with the sweet Prädikat wines and botrytis selections hanging on into November. Several leading estates farm organically or biodynamically, and old Traminer and Riesling vines are prized. The carting of crushed basalt onto the sandstone at Forst is the region's most quoted piece of soil engineering, a reminder that terroir here includes two centuries of human editing.
made.winemaking: The Pfalz is a dry wine region first. Riesling is fermented to dryness, often in stainless steel but frequently in the big neutral oak casks, the Stückfass and Doppelstück, that the old estates have always used, and the top wines rest on their lees through the winter. Grosses Gewächs bottlings are released the following September or later and are built for the cellar. The Pinot family is handled in the Burgundian way, Spätburgunder with some whole bunches and barriques, Weissburgunder with lees stirring and a little oak. Dornfelder is made soft and fruity for early drinking or, at the serious end, with barrel ageing. Residual sugar survives only where the grower wants it: a sweet Kabinett or Spätlese is a choice here, not a necessity, and the botrytis wines from Scheurebe and Rieslaner are small, deliberate selections. Grower Sekt by the traditional method is a long Mittelhaardt tradition.

places.name: Mittelhaardt
places.note: The northern Bereich, officially Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstrasse, is the historic core: a line of villages on sandstone, loam and limestone at the foot of the Haardt around Bad Dürkheim and Neustadt. The Bavarian tax survey of 1828 ranked these sites, and the ranking still shapes prices. Full, dry Riesling is its signature.

places.name: Forst an der Weinstrasse
places.note: The village whose growers carted black basalt from the Pechsteinkopf onto their sandstone vineyards, giving dense, smoky, long lived Riesling. Its named sites are the most famous in the Pfalz.

places.name: Kirchenstück
places.note: A small walled site beside the church that the 1828 survey placed at the very top of the Pfalz; the most complete and expensive Forst Riesling.

places.name: Jesuitengarten
places.note: The rounder, more perfumed neighbour of Kirchenstück, once the property of the Jesuits, as the name records.

places.name: Ungeheuer
places.note: The monster, a large and powerful site giving broad, spicy Riesling that needs time in bottle.

places.name: Pechstein
places.note: Named for the black basalt it sits on; the smokiest and most savoury Forst wine, with a flinty edge.

places.name: Deidesheim
places.note: A handsome small town with limestone and sandstone sites such as Hohenmorgen, Kalkofen, Grainhübel and Langenmorgen, home to several historic estates. Its Riesling is a shade more elegant and floral than Forst's.

places.name: Hohenmorgen
places.note: A compact limestone and sandstone site on the slope towards Forst, prized for fine, mineral, age-worthy Riesling.

places.name: Kalkofen
places.note: The lime kiln: limestone close to the surface gives taut, chalky Riesling that stands apart from the basalt wines next door.

places.name: Ruppertsberg
places.note: South of Deidesheim, with the Reiterpfad and the monopole Gaisböhl; gravelly, sandy sites giving earlier drinking, fruit forward Riesling.

places.name: Wachenheim
places.note: North of Forst, with Gerümpel, Rechbächel and Goldbächel; the home village of one of the region's great historic estates and a source of firm, slightly leaner Riesling.

places.name: Bad Dürkheim
places.note: The spa town at the centre of the Mittelhaardt, with the Michelsberg and Spielberg sites and the Wurstmarkt, the enormous September wine festival.

places.name: Kallstadt
places.note: A limestone village north of Bad Dürkheim whose Saumagen vineyard, sharing its name with the stuffed pig's stomach dish of the Pfalz, gives chalky, long lived dry Riesling.

places.name: Haardt, Gimmeldingen and Königsbach
places.note: Villages above Neustadt with the Bürgergarten, Mandelgarten and Idig sites; the southern Mittelhaardt, where Riesling meets Scheurebe, Rieslaner and Spätburgunder.

places.name: Neustadt an der Weinstrasse
places.note: The region's wine capital at the join of the two Bereiche, with the research institute at Mussbach.

places.name: Laumersheim and the Zellertal
places.note: The northern Pfalz towards Rheinhessen, on limestone and loess, where Spätburgunder and Riesling from Kirschgarten and the Schwarzer Herrgott have earned a modern reputation.

places.name: Südliche Weinstrasse
places.note: The southern Bereich from Neustadt to the French border, warmer and more varied in soil, long a source of bulk wine and now home to some of the region's finest estates. The Pinot family, Riesling on red slate and limestone, and Spätburgunder from Schweigen are the modern story.

places.name: Birkweiler
places.note: A village west of Landau whose Kastanienbusch, on red slate, gives among the most mineral dry Riesling in the Pfalz; the Mandelberg is its limestone neighbour.

places.name: Siebeldingen
places.note: Beside Birkweiler, with the Im Sonnenschein site of limestone and the vine breeding institute at Geilweilerhof, which bred Regent.

places.name: Schweigen
places.note: The last village before France, at the Deutsches Weintor; much of its Sonnenberg vineyard, with the Kammerberg and Sankt Paul parcels, lies in France, and the grapes are vinified in Germany as German wine.

places.name: Rhodt unter Rietburg
places.note: A village below the Rietburg ruin keeping ancient Traminer vines in its Rosengarten, a reminder that Gewürztraminer is an old Pfalz grape.

places.name: Landau in der Pfalz
places.note: The market town of the south, ringed by loess and loam vineyards that fill much of the region's everyday Dornfelder and Grauburgunder.

producers.name: Dr. Bürklin-Wolf
producers.why: The great biodynamic Mittelhaardt estate at Wachenheim, with the top Forst sites and a label hierarchy drawn from the 1828 Bavarian tax survey.

producers.name: Müller-Catoir
producers.why: The Haardt house that keeps Rieslaner and Scheurebe alive as serious wines, and the name to reach for when a question moves beyond Riesling.

producers.name: Reichsrat von Buhl
producers.why: A Deidesheim house and one of the three Bs of the Mittelhaardt with Bassermann-Jordan and Bürklin-Wolf, known for Forst Riesling GG and for traditional method Sekt.

producers.name: Bassermann-Jordan
producers.why: The Deidesheim estate with deep holdings in Forst and Deidesheim and one of the longest histories in the region.

producers.name: A. Christmann
producers.why: Gimmeldingen estate farming biodynamically, with the Königsbacher Idig as its flagship GG.

producers.name: Georg Mosbacher
producers.why: A Forst grower whose Ungeheuer, Pechstein and Kirchenstück show the village at the top of its game.

producers.name: Koehler-Ruprecht
producers.why: Kallstadt estate famous for long cask aged, dry Saumagen Riesling released years after the harvest.

producers.name: Ökonomierat Rebholz
producers.why: Siebeldingen pioneer of bone dry, unchaptalised Riesling and Spätburgunder from the Kastanienbusch and Im Sonnenschein.

producers.name: Dr. Wehrheim
producers.why: Birkweiler house whose Kastanienbusch Riesling and Weissburgunder put the red slate of the south on the map.

producers.name: Friedrich Becker
producers.why: Schweigen estate with Spätburgunder from the Kammerberg and Sankt Paul parcels of the Sonnenberg, which lie on the French side of the border.

producers.name: Knipser
producers.why: Laumersheim estate that led the northern Pfalz into serious Spätburgunder and dry Riesling.

terroir.climate: The Haardt, the northern continuation of the Vosges, wrings the rain out of the westerly weather before it reaches the vines, so the Pfalz sits in a rain shadow. It is one of the driest and sunniest corners of Germany, with mild winters and long, warm summers; figs, almonds, lemons and kiwi fruit grow along the wine road. Riesling ripens fully here in almost every year, which is why the region's natural style is dry. Drought in a hot summer is a greater hazard than rot.
terroir.soils: Weathered sandstone washed down from the Haardt gives the Mittelhaardt its light, warm, free-draining base, mixed with loam, loess and gravel on the lower ground. Limestone surfaces at Deidesheim, Kallstadt and widely across the south. At Forst, black basalt from the Pechsteinkopf outcrop above the village was quarried and spread over the vineyards for generations to darken and warm the soil. In the Südliche Weinstrasse, Birkweiler's Kastanienbusch adds red slate to a palette of loess, loam and shell limestone.
terroir.topography: The vineyards lie on the gentle eastern slopes and foothills where the forested Haardt drops to the Rhine plain, mostly between roughly 100 and 250 metres. The ridge shelters them from the west and the flat plain spreads east towards the Rhine, which is some kilometres away. There is nothing here like the Mosel's cliffs: the best sites are modest slopes at the edge of the forest that catch the morning sun and drain fast.
terroir.water: The Rhine is too far east to shape the vineyards directly, so the Pfalz's water story is the shortage of it: shelter and dryness rather than a river's reflected light.

traps: Pfalz is not Palatinate wine of the sweet 1970s kind: today the region is dry first, and its Riesling is among Germany's fullest.
The Haardt is the hill range and Haardt is also a village above Neustadt; the shelter comes from the range.
Forst's basalt was quarried and spread by hand; it is not the bedrock of the whole village.
Mittelhaardt is a Bereich of the Pfalz, not a region of its own, and Südliche Weinstrasse is the other, not a wine road only.
Dornfelder is a 1955 Weinsberg crossing from Württemberg, though the Pfalz and Rheinhessen grow most of it.
Schweigen's best Spätburgunder parcels lie in France; the wine is still German Qualitätswein.
Grosses Gewächs since 2021 is also a legal term; the VDP's eagle marks only its members' wines.

wines.note: Dry, ripe Riesling of yellow peach, smoke and spice with a firm acid spine. Serve cool rather than cold, and reach for it with pork, roast chicken or anything with a little spice.
The dry top wine of a single classified site, picked at least at Spätlese ripeness and often built to keep for a decade. Forst and Deidesheim are the names a guest will recognise.
Lightly sweet Pfalz Riesling is riper and broader than the Mosel's and less common than it was; it carries chilli and ginger well.
Pfalz Pinot Noir is darker and warmer than the Ahr's, with ripe cherry and spice and real tannin from the limestone sites of the south. A fine partner for duck or lamb.
Dry Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris, creamy and nutty, the region's answer to a guest who wants an unoaked Chardonnay style.
Deep purple, soft and plummy, sometimes with a little residual sugar; the everyday red of the Pfalz and good with grilled sausages.
Botrytised sweet wines from the aromatic crossings, grapefruit and blackcurrant in Scheurebe, steel and apricot in Rieslaner, with acidity that keeps them from cloying.
Grower sparkling wine from Riesling or the Pinot family by the traditional method; the Pfalz is one of its strongholds and serves it as an aperitif.

exam: Geography first: the west running Rhine, the Taunus wall, the south facing bank; Hochheim on the Main, Assmannshausen at the gorge.
Style against the Mosel: fuller, drier, firmer, higher must weight floors, more Spätburgunder.
The dates the exam likes: Eberbach 1136, Johannisberg's Spätlese 1775, Charta 1984, Erstes Gewächs 1999.
Villages west to east with a site each; Schloss Johannisberg, Schloss Vollrads and Steinberg as Ortsteile.
Hock and its origin; Geisenheim and Müller-Thurgau's birth in 1882.
For Advanced: the soil shift from slate to loess to phyllite along the slope, and Rauenthal's late ripening.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Nearly four fifths of the vineyard: dry, firm, peach and quince with a smoky grip, from Charta and Erstes Gewächs to GG, and the botrytis Auslese, BA and TBA that the region named.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Spätburgunder, about one vine in eight, concentrated at Assmannshausen on the Höllenberg's slate: dry, oak aged, red cherry and earth.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Bred at Geisenheim in 1882 and planted on the flatter ground: soft, floral, early.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder in small plots, dry and creamy, a food white beside the Riesling.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A little, mostly for Sekt and a few oaked dry whites.

law.classification: The Rheingau is a single Bereich, Johannisberg, with a handful of Grosslagen such as Johannisberger Erntebringer and Rüdesheimer Burgweg, and its minimum must weights sit above the Mosel's: for Riesling, Kabinett 73 degrees Oechsle, Spätlese 85, Auslese 95, Beerenauslese and Eiswein 125, Trockenbeerenauslese 150. Four estates hold Ortsteil status and are labelled without a village: Schloss Johannisberg, Schloss Vollrads, Steinberg and Schloss Reichartshausen. The region wrote its own first growth law: the Charta association of 1984 led to the state of Hesse recognising Erstes Gewächs in 1999 for dry Riesling and Spätburgunder from classified sites, the only such legal term in Germany for two decades. The VDP's Rheingau members moved to Grosses Gewächs from the 2012 vintage, and the federal law of 2021 makes both Erstes Gewächs and Grosses Gewächs national terms for dry single vineyard wine.
labels: The old English word for Rhine wine, from Hochheim.
A castle estate; Schloss Johannisberg and Schloss Vollrads are Ortsteile labelled without a village name.
Wine of the Steinberg, Kloster Eberbach's walled vineyard, an Ortsteil of Hattenheim.
The Rhine's twelve hundred litre cask.
The whole Rheingau as one district; a district blend, not a Johannisberg wine.
tiers: Quality wine from the region; may be chaptalised; the dry everyday bottle.
Rheingau floors for Riesling: 73, 85, 95, 125, 125 and 150 degrees Oechsle, higher than the Mosel's at every step.
The growers' standard of 1984: Riesling only, dry or halbtrocken, picked riper than the law asks, from Rheingau sites, the double Romanesque arch on the bottle.
The Rheingau's legal first growth from 1999: dry Riesling or Spätburgunder from classified sites, tasted by a panel; now a national term under the 2021 law.
The VDP's top site and its dry wine, used by Rheingau members since the 2012 vintage in place of Erstes Gewächs.

made.viticulture: The Rheingau trains Riesling on wires, one or two canes in the Guyot manner, and the gentler central slopes can be worked by tractor; only the slate walls of the Rüdesheimer Berg and Assmannshausen ask for the Mosel's hand labour. Land consolidation in the twentieth century terraced and reshaped much of the slope. Clonal selection is a local science: the research and teaching institute at Geisenheim, founded in 1872, bred Müller-Thurgau in 1882 and supplies the Riesling clones most of Germany plants. Harvest runs from late September into November, with selective passes for the Prädikate and a watch on the river mists that bring botrytis; frost at the forest edge, hail and downy mildew in a wet summer are the hazards. The Spätlese legend of 1775 belongs here: the courier bringing the abbot's permission to pick at Johannisberg arrived late, the grapes had rotted on the vine, and the wine was the best anyone had made. Yields for Erstes Gewächs and GG are capped well below the regional norm.
made.winemaking: The Rhine's cask is the Stück, twelve hundred litres of old oak, though stainless steel now does most of the fermenting. The region's modern identity is dry: the Charta growers of 1984 set a standard for trocken and halbtrocken Riesling picked at higher must weight, and the Erstes Gewächs rules that followed in 1999 asked for classified sites, dry wine and a tasting panel. Fermentation runs to the end at 12 to 13 per cent, malolactic is avoided to keep the acid line, and the wines rest on their lees into spring; a GG waits until 1 September of the year after harvest. The sweet tradition continues from Kabinett to TBA by stopping the ferment or by botrytis concentration, with Eiswein in the cold years. Assmannshausen's Pinot Noir is fermented in open vats and aged in barrique, a style the state domaine kept alive when no one else in Germany made serious red. Eltville houses several sparkling wine cellars working the traditional method on Riesling.

places.name: Lorch
places.note: Beyond the bend, in the Mittelrhein gorge but legally Rheingau: slate, steep, Riesling late and lean; Bodental-Steinberg and Krone.

places.name: Assmannshausen
places.note: Where the river turns north: the Höllenberg, slate and phyllite, the home of Rheingau Spätburgunder for centuries and the state domaine's red cellar.

places.name: Rüdesheim
places.note: The Rüdesheimer Berg, the steep western end on slate and quartzite above the river: Berg Schlossberg, the finest and driest, Berg Roseneck and Berg Rottland; Bischofsberg, Drachenstein and Klosterlay on gentler ground. Ripe even in cool years.

places.name: Geisenheim
places.note: Rothenberg and Kläuserweg on loess tinged with slate, and the research and teaching institute of 1872 where Müller-Thurgau was bred; Johannisberg is one of its districts.

places.name: Johannisberg
places.note: Schloss Johannisberg above the village, Benedictine from about 1100, planted to Riesling alone from 1720 and the birthplace of the Spätlese in 1775; the castle is an Ortsteil. Hölle and Klaus lie beside it.

places.name: Winkel
places.note: Jesuitengarten and Hasensprung on loess and loam: ripe, generous Riesling; Schloss Vollrads above the village, selling wine since 1211, is an Ortsteil.

places.name: Oestrich
places.note: Lenchen and Doosberg, broad sites near the river with the old wine crane on the bank: ripe, fruity Riesling and fine Auslese.

places.name: Hallgarten
places.note: The highest village, cool, late and firm: Schönhell and Jungfer give Riesling with acid and length.

places.name: Hattenheim
places.note: Wisselbrunnen, Nussbrunnen and Mannberg on marl near the river, and above the village Kloster Eberbach, the Cistercian abbey of 1136, whose walled Steinberg is an Ortsteil labelled Steinberger. The Marcobrunn spring marks the border with Erbach.

places.name: Erbach
places.note: Marcobrunn, the brook of the border, on marl and loess by the river, long held the Rheingau's richest, most honeyed Riesling; Siegelsberg and Schlossberg beside it.

places.name: Kiedrich
places.note: Set back from the river on phyllite and slate: the Gräfenberg, spicy and racy, among the finest Riesling and TBA sites in Germany; Turmberg and Wasseros beside it.

places.name: Rauenthal
places.note: High above Eltville, late ripening and spicy: Baiken, Gehrn, Rothenberg and Nonnenberg give Rieslings that need years.

places.name: Eltville
places.note: The largest wine town, with the cellars of the Hessian state domaine and the sparkling houses; Sonnenberg and Langenstück on the slope.

places.name: Walluf
places.note: The eastern village before Wiesbaden; the Walkenberg and old Riesling parcels.

places.name: Hochheim
places.note: Apart on the Main east of Wiesbaden, on limestone and marl: Domdechaney, Kirchenstück, Hölle and Königin Victoriaberg, named for the queen's visit of 1845; rounder, earthier wines and the source of the word Hock.

producers.name: Schloss Johannisberg
producers.why: The Riesling monastery of 1720 and the Spätlese of 1775; its coloured capsules have coded the Prädikate since the nineteenth century.

producers.name: Schloss Vollrads
producers.why: Winkel; wine sold since 1211, a moated tower and dry Riesling in the Charta mould.

producers.name: Robert Weil
producers.why: Kiedrich; the Gräfenberg from dry GG to TBA, the Rheingau's reference for botrytis wine since the 1990s.

producers.name: Georg Breuer
producers.why: Rüdesheim; Berg Schlossberg and Nonnenberg, bone dry Riesling that led the Charta idea to its conclusion.

producers.name: Hessische Staatsweingüter Kloster Eberbach
producers.why: The state domaine at the abbey; Steinberg, Assmannshausen's Höllenberg reds and the abbey's medieval cellars.

producers.name: Künstler
producers.why: Hochheim; Domdechaney, Kirchenstück and Hölle, the proof that the Main's limestone makes grand dry Riesling.

producers.name: Leitz
producers.why: Rüdesheim; the Berg sites parcel by parcel, dry and sweet, widely poured by the glass.

producers.name: August Kesseler
producers.why: Assmannshausen; Höllenberg Spätburgunder that set the modern standard for Rheingau red.

producers.name: Peter Jakob Kühn
producers.why: Oestrich; biodynamic, long lees ageing, Doosberg and Lenchen with unusual depth.

terroir.climate: Cool continental tempered by the river and shielded by the Taunus, whose forested ridge stops the north wind; the south facing bank gathers sun all day and the Rhine, broad and slow here, reflects it back. Autumn mists off the water bring botrytis for Auslese and above, and the long season lets Riesling ripen fully while keeping its acid. Rainfall is moderate; the sites nearest the river are warmest, the ones up towards the forest coolest and latest.
terroir.soils: Varied along the slope: at Rüdesheim and Assmannshausen in the west, slate and Taunus quartzite on steep ground, which is why Pinot Noir and the fieriest Riesling live there; through the centre, from Geisenheim to Erbach, deep loess and loam over sandstone and marl, giving the broad, ripe style of Johannisberg and Marcobrunn; at Kiedrich and Rauenthal, phyllite and slate on higher ground, spicy and mineral; at Hochheim, Tertiary limestone and marl beside the Main.
terroir.topography: A long, gentle south facing slope rather than a gorge: the vines rise from the river terrace at about 80 metres to around 300 metres at the forest edge, steepest at the western end where the Rüdesheimer Berg drops to the river and the Rhine itself turns north through the Binger Loch into the Mittelrhein gorge past Assmannshausen and Lorch. The villages sit in a line along the foot of the slope; the best sites are mid-slope.
terroir.water: The Rhine, flowing east to west for the length of the region, moderating frost, storing warmth and lighting the slope; its width here matters more than anywhere else in Germany. The Main joins it at Mainz; Hochheim's vines, a few kilometres up the smaller river, face the Main rather than the Rhine. Mists off both feed botrytis.

traps: Erstes Gewächs was the Rheingau's own legal first growth, not the VDP's Erste Lage: cousins, not twins.
Hochheim is on the Main, not the Rhine, and belongs to the Rheingau all the same.
Steinberg is a vineyard, not a village; Steinberger on a label is an Ortsteil of Hattenheim.
Marcobrunn sits on the border of Hattenheim and Erbach and is labelled Erbacher.
Assmannshausen is the red island of a Riesling region, on slate; do not put Rheingau Spätburgunder at Johannisberg.
A Rheingau Kabinett needs 73 degrees Oechsle, not the Mosel's 70: each region sets its own floor.

wines.note: The regional staple: dry, medium bodied, peach and quince with a smoky edge, 12 to 13 per cent; with pork schnitzel, roast chicken, river fish and asparagus.

Dry Riesling from a classified site such as Rüdesheimer Berg Schlossberg, Kiedricher Gräfenberg or Erbacher Marcobrunn: firm, long, built for ten years; decant it young and serve it with richer fish and veal.
Lightly sweet and fuller than the Mosel's at 9 to 11 per cent, apricot and honey over stone; a Spätlese with spiced pork or a fruit stuffed bird.
The botrytis tradition the Rheingau named: Spätlese and Auslese were coined at Johannisberg, and a TBA from Kiedrich or Rauenthal is among the longest lived sweet wines in the world.
Pinot Noir from the Höllenberg's slate: pale to medium ruby, red cherry, earth and smoke, dry and oak aged; with duck, lamb and game.
Riesling base wine from the cooler sites by the traditional method, lean and lively; an aperitif and the house pour at Eltville's sparkling cellars.
From the Main rather than the Rhine, on limestone and marl: rounder, earthier, the wine the English called Hock.

exam: Size and shape: the largest region, the triangle Mainz, Worms, Bingen, three Bereiche.
Two faces: Liebfraumilch and Gutes Domtal against the Roter Hang and the Wonnegau.
The Liebfraumilch rule as the law writes it: four regions, four grapes, 70 per cent, lieblich.
Sites and villages: Nierstein and Nackenheim on red slate, Westhofen and Dalsheim on limestone.
Grapes beyond Riesling: Silvaner's largest home, Scheurebe's birth at Alzey, Dornfelder's volume.
For Advanced: Bingen's Scharlachberg, Ingelheim's Pinot, Siefersheim's porphyry, the Glöck of 742.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The leading grape by area in the 2020s: dry, ripe, salty on the Wonnegau's limestone, smoky and spicy on the Roter Hang's red slate, with Kabinett, Spätlese and botrytis Auslese from the river sites.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: The former leader and still a large share: soft, floral, early white, the base of much Liebfraumilch.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.styles: The volume red: deep coloured, soft, plummy, dry or off dry.

grapes.name: Silvaner
grapes.styles: Rheinhessen holds more Silvaner than any region in the world: earthy, pear and hay, dry, the asparagus wine of spring.

grapes.name: Scheurebe
grapes.styles: Bred at Alzey in 1916: blackcurrant and pink grapefruit, dry or as a honeyed Auslese.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grauburgunder on loess: round, nutty, dry, the everyday food white.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder, dry and creamy, sometimes with oak.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Spätburgunder on the limestone, with Ingelheim as its old home: cherry, dry, light to medium bodied.

law.classification: The national ladder applies across three Bereiche: Bingen in the north west, Nierstein along the Rheinterrasse and Wonnegau in the south. The Grosslagen made the region's old name, Niersteiner Gutes Domtal above all, a collective label centred on the flat land of Dexheim with hardly a vine on Nierstein's slope, and Oppenheimer Krötenbrunnen and Bingen St. Rochuskapelle beside it; Nierstein's own slope sites fall under the smaller Grosslagen Rehbach, Auflangen and Spiegelberg. Liebfraumilch is defined in law as a lieblich Qualitätswein from Rheinhessen, the Pfalz, the Nahe or the Rheingau, at least 70 per cent Riesling, Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau or Kerner, named for the Liebfrauenkirche at Worms. The VDP's Rheinhessen members classify the Roter Hang and the Wonnegau's limestone hills as Grosse Lage and bottle dry Riesling Grosses Gewächs from them. Under the 2021 federal law the Grosslagen take the word Region from the 2026 vintage.
labels: A lieblich Qualitätswein from four Rhine regions, at least 70 per cent Riesling, Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau or Kerner.
A Grosslage over flat land around Dexheim that borrows Nierstein's name; not a Nierstein slope wine.
The red slope: the Rotliegend escarpment from Nackenheim to Nierstein.
The name for the river front strip from Bodenheim south through Nackenheim, Nierstein and Oppenheim.
Müller-Thurgau under a drier sounding name.
tiers: Quality wine from the region; may be chaptalised; the base of Liebfraumilch and the dry everyday bottle.
Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese by must weight, from the Roter Hang and the river villages above all.

Pettenthal, Hipping, Brudersberg, Ölberg, Orbel, Rothenberg, Morstein, Kirchspiel, Brunnenhäuschen, Aulerde, Hubacker, Kirchenstück, Heerkretz, Scharlachberg among the classified sites; the dry Riesling from one is the GG.
The three districts; a Bereich name on a label is a district blend, labelled as a Region from the 2026 vintage.

made.viticulture: Most of Rheinhessen is gentle enough for machines, trained on wires at moderate density, and the flat, fertile river land was long cropped for volume; the revival has been a matter of choosing the slopes and the rock instead. On the Roter Hang the red sandstone is steep, hand worked and warm, and ripens early; in the Wonnegau the limestone hills are cooler than their latitude suggests, and growers there pick late into October for ripe skins at modest sugar. Drought is the modern hazard on the loess and sand, frost in the hollows the old one; botrytis comes with the river mists at Nierstein and Nackenheim and is used for Auslese. Yields on the classified sites are cut far below the regional norm, and several leading houses farm biodynamically. The breeding station at Alzey, where Scheurebe was crossed in 1916, gave the region many of the crossings that filled its flat land; Riesling has since taken the lead from Müller-Thurgau by area.
made.winemaking: Two cellars share the region. The volume cellar ferments cool in stainless steel, chaptalises its Qualitätswein where the law allows, back sweetens with Süssreserve to the lieblich band and bottles young: Liebfraumilch, Niersteiner Gutes Domtal, soft Dornfelder. The quality cellar presses whole bunches gently, ferments with wild yeasts in old oak casks or steel, leaves the dry Riesling on its lees for months, sometimes a year, and bottles it dry at 12.5 to 13.5 per cent with under 9 grams of sugar for the GG, which waits until 1 September of the year after harvest. Silvaner and the Pinots are made dry, some with a share of barrel. The Prädikat wines of the Roter Hang are stopped by chilling for Kabinett and Spätlese and left to botrytis for Auslese and above; a gold capsule marks a house's richer lot. Spätburgunder at Ingelheim and in the Wonnegau goes through open vats and barrique in the Burgundian manner.

places.name: Rheinterrasse and the Roter Hang (Bereich Nierstein)
places.note: The river front where the plateau falls to the Rhine: a short, steep escarpment of red Permian Rotliegend sandstone and slate from Nackenheim to Nierstein, warm, early and smoky, with limestone and loess continuing south through Oppenheim.

places.name: Nackenheim
places.note: The northern end of the Roter Hang: the Rothenberg, red slate falling to the river, gives the Rhine's spiciest Riesling.

places.name: Nierstein
places.note: The heart of the red slope: Pettenthal, Hipping, Brudersberg, Ölberg and Orbel on the Rotliegend, and the Glöck, documented in 742 and the oldest named vineyard in Germany. The Grosslage Gutes Domtal borrows the town's name for flat land at Dexheim.

places.name: Oppenheim
places.note: Sackträger and Kreuz on limestone and loess south of Nierstein, below the Katharinenkirche: rounder, riper Riesling.

places.name: Wonnegau
places.note: The southern Bereich around Worms and Alzey: rolling limestone and clay hills, cooler than they look, where dry Riesling of weight and salt has made the region's modern name.

places.name: Westhofen
places.note: Morstein, limestone over clay and the grandest of the Wonnegau; Kirchspiel, a south east facing bowl; Brunnenhäuschen and Aulerde: dry Riesling of weight and precision.

places.name: Flörsheim-Dalsheim
places.note: Hubacker and Bürgel on limestone and marl, the Dalsheim side of the Wonnegau's fame, with Auslese and TBA beside the dry wines.

places.name: Hohen-Sülzen and Mölsheim
places.note: Kirchenstück and the Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott, limestone sites on the Pfalz border, dry and taut.

places.name: Worms
places.note: The Liebfrauenkirche's own vineyard, the Liebfrauenstift-Kirchenstück, where Liebfraumilch began as a single wine before the name went generic across four regions.

places.name: Bereich Bingen
places.note: The north west, from the Nahe's mouth up the Rhine towards Mainz: quartzite and slate above Bingen, limestone at Ingelheim, loess between.

places.name: Bingen
places.note: The Scharlachberg, quartzite and slate on the Rochusberg above the Nahe's mouth, facing the Rheingau across the river: firm, mineral Riesling.

places.name: Ingelheim
places.note: The old red wine town, with Charlemagne's palace and Spätburgunder on limestone: the Pinot tradition of Rheinhessen.

places.name: Rheinhessische Schweiz
places.note: The hilly west around Siefersheim: volcanic porphyry under Heerkretz and Höllberg, smoky, taut Riesling far from the river.

places.name: Alzey
places.note: The inland town at the centre of the triangle and the breeding station where Scheurebe was crossed in 1916.

places.name: Mainz
places.note: The capital at the northern corner, the printing city, with the region's wine fairs and the Rhine's bend below it.

terroir.climate: The driest and one of the warmest parts of Germany, sheltered by the Hunsrück, the Taunus and the Donnersberg, with around 500 millimetres of rain a year and plenty of sun; continental in the interior and river tempered on the Rheinterrasse. Drought on the lighter soils and spring frost in the hollows are the hazards; ripening is easy, so the task is acidity and restraint.
terroir.soils: Loess over much of the hills; limestone, marl and clay in the Wonnegau to the south, under Morstein, Kirchspiel and Hubacker; the red Permian Rotliegend sandstone and slate of the Roter Hang at Nierstein and Nackenheim; quartzite and slate at Bingen's Scharlachberg; volcanic porphyry at Siefersheim in the hilly west; and sand and gravel on the flat river land that fed the old bulk trade.
terroir.topography: A plateau of rolling hills, mostly between 100 and 250 metres, falling in a short, steep red escarpment to the Rhine between Nackenheim and Nierstein, the Rheinterrasse, and rising west into the Rheinhessische Schweiz around Siefersheim. The triangle is drawn by Mainz in the north, Worms in the south and Bingen in the west, with Alzey at its centre.
terroir.water: The Rhine forms the eastern and northern edge, reflecting light onto the Roter Hang and moderating the river villages; the Selz and the Pfrimm are small inland streams. Most of the region lies far enough from water to be truly continental.

traps: Rheinhessen is not the Rheingau: it lies inside the Rhine's bend, flat and rolling, not on the Taunus slope.
Niersteiner Gutes Domtal is a Grosslage with almost no vines in Nierstein; Niersteiner Pettenthal is the real thing.
Liebfraumilch may come from four regions and never from the Mosel; it must be lieblich, never trocken.
The Roter Hang is red sandstone and slate of the Permian age, not volcanic rock; Siefersheim's porphyry is the volcanic one.
Silvaner is the region's traditional grape, not Riesling; Riesling took the lead from Müller-Thurgau only in recent decades.
Westhofen's Morstein is in the Wonnegau, not on the Rheinterrasse: limestone, not red slate.

wines.note: The modern face: dry, ripe, 12.5 to 13.5 per cent, yellow fruit and herbs with a salty finish from the limestone; with pork, poultry, asparagus and a fish stew.
From the red sandstone slope by the Rhine: smoky, spicy and firm, often dry, sometimes Kabinett or Spätlese; the red rock lends a red fruit note to a white wine.
wines.style: Roter Hang Riesling (Niersteiner Pettenthal, Hipping, Nackenheimer Rothenberg)

wines.note: Limestone Riesling of weight and precision, among the most expensive dry whites in Germany; wait five years and serve it with turbot or veal.
wines.style: Wonnegau Riesling Grosses Gewächs (Morstein, Kirchspiel, Hubacker)

wines.note: Dry, earthy, pear and hay with soft acid; the classic partner for white asparagus in spring.
Blackcurrant, grapefruit and cassis leaf, dry or as a honeyed Auslese; with spiced and aromatic dishes.
Botrytis from the river mists on the Rheinterrasse or late picked in the Wonnegau: rich, honeyed, with a gold capsule from the best houses.
A lieblich Qualitätswein, at least 70 per cent Riesling, Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau or Kerner, from Rheinhessen, Pfalz, Nahe or Rheingau: soft, sweetish and simple, the history rather than the future.
Deep coloured, soft, plummy red bred for the home market; dry or off dry, served cool.
The old red wine town's Pinot Noir on limestone: cherry, dry, light to medium bodied.

exam: Place Württemberg: the Neckar and its tributaries around Stuttgart and Heilbronn, south east of the Rhine regions.
Say the signature: Germany's red wine region, more red than white, Trollinger for everyday and Lemberger for serious.
Decode the synonyms: Trollinger is Schiava, Lemberger is Blaufränkisch, Schwarzriesling is Pinot Meunier.
Know Schillerwein as a Rotling, red and white grapes fermented together, protected to Württemberg.
Know Weinsberg, founded 1868, as the school that bred Kerner (1929) and Dornfelder (1955).
Name the six Bereiche and remember the Bayerischer Bodensee sits in Bavaria yet belongs to this region.
Know Keuper marl and Muschelkalk terraces as the soils, and the cooperatives as the makers.

grapes.name: Trollinger
grapes.styles: The region's everyday red, pale, light, soft and often a touch sweet, drunk young and cool by the quarter litre; Schiava or Vernatsch in the Alto Adige.

grapes.name: Lemberger
grapes.styles: Blaufränkisch under its Württemberg name: the serious red, dark fruited, peppery and firm, dry and increasingly barrel aged, and admitted to the VDP's Grosses Gewächs here.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The main white, dry and firm from the Neckar terraces and the Remstal, with more body than the Mosel's.

grapes.name: Schwarzriesling
grapes.styles: Pinot Meunier, called black Riesling though it is no Riesling; a soft, pale red speciality.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Spätburgunder from the best Keuper and limestone slopes is the modern ambition alongside Lemberger.

grapes.name: Samtrot
grapes.styles: A velvety red mutation of Schwarzriesling selected at Weinsberg, a Württemberg curiosity.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.styles: Bred at Weinsberg in 1955 for colour; deep, soft reds for the everyday table.

grapes.name: Kerner
grapes.styles: The 1929 Weinsberg crossing of Trollinger and Riesling, a reliable aromatic white.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Simple, soft dry whites from the easier ground, often sold as Rivaner.

law.classification: Württemberg is one of the thirteen Anbaugebiete, so its Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein carry the region's name and an official test number, ranked by must weight at harvest from Qualitätswein through the Prädikat ladder, with the 2021 reform's origin pyramid of Anbaugebiet, Region, Ort and Einzellage laid over it and Erstes Gewächs and Grosses Gewächs as protected dry single site terms, binding in full from the 2026 vintage. The region has six Bereiche: Remstal-Stuttgart, Württembergisch Unterland, Kocher-Jagst-Tauber, Oberer Neckar, Württembergischer Bodensee and, across the state line, Bayerischer Bodensee. Schillerwein is a Rotling protected to Württemberg at Qualitätswein level or above. Within the VDP's private pyramid the region's Grosses Gewächs admits Lemberger alongside Riesling and Spätburgunder, so the Blaufränkisch synonym appears on top tier German labels.
labels: A Württemberg Rotling: red and white grapes fermented together, Qualitätswein or above.
A rosé from one named red variety, Qualitätswein or above.
The regional name for Blaufränkisch; Limberger is a permitted spelling.
The regional name for the grape the Alto Adige calls Schiava or Vernatsch.
The quarter litre glass in which the region drinks its Trollinger.
A grower's seasonal tavern, marked by a broom over the door, allowed to open and sell its own wine for a limited number of weeks each year.
Legally dry, at most 4 grams per litre of sugar or up to 9 where acidity is within 2 grams of it.
tiers: The protected geographical indication level, here Schwäbischer Landwein.
Quality wine from Württemberg alone, test number required, enrichment allowed within zone A.
Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese by must weight at picking; a Trollinger Kabinett is a common sight and is often lightly sweet.

Protected terms for dry wine of protected origin from a named single vineyard: the ordinance caps Erstes Gewächs at 60 hectolitres per hectare, 70 on steep slopes, and holds Grosses Gewächs to a lower cap, hand picking and a later release.
The association's top site class; Lemberger, Riesling and Spätburgunder are the grapes seen as GG here.

made.viticulture: Württemberg's vines are planted mostly in red grapes, which only the tiny Ahr otherwise matches, and they are tended by thousands of small growers who deliver to cooperatives; the cooperative share of the crop is among the largest in the country. The old terraces along the Neckar, Hessigheim's Felsengärten and the walls at Besigheim and Mundelsheim among them, are narrow, steep and hand worked, and keeping them alive is the region's running struggle; the Keuper hills are mechanised. Trollinger ripens very late and needs the warmest ground, which is why it was planted where Lemberger and Spätburgunder would now do better, and high yields long kept it pale and simple. Frost on low ground and hail are the hazards. The state school at Weinsberg, founded in 1868, bred Kerner in 1929 and Dornfelder in 1955 and selected Samtrot, so the region's grape list carries its own research history. Harvest runs from late September into November for the latest Trollinger.
made.winemaking: Most Württemberg wine is made by cooperatives at scale and drunk within the region, so the traditional style is light: Trollinger sees a short maceration, little or no oak and often a touch of residual sugar, and is bottled young. Schillerwein is made by fermenting red and white grapes together, a Rotling, and Weissherbst by pressing a single red variety as rosé. The serious work is in Lemberger and Spätburgunder, where a generation of estates picks lower yields, ferments with longer maceration and ages in barrique, producing Grosses Gewächs reds that the rest of Germany now takes seriously. Riesling is fermented dry, usually in stainless steel. Sekt by the traditional method is a growing side line, and the Besen, the grower's seasonal tavern marked by a broom over the door, remains the natural place to taste the region's wine with its food.

places.name: Remstal-Stuttgart
places.note: The Bereich around the state capital and the Rems valley to its east, on Keuper marl. Stuttgart has vineyards inside its city limits, and Fellbach, Untertürkheim and the Remstal villages hold several of the region's leading estates for Lemberger, Riesling and Spätburgunder.

places.name: Fellbach
places.note: A town at the edge of Stuttgart whose Lämmler site on Keuper is a reference for Lemberger and Riesling Grosses Gewächs.

places.name: Untertürkheim and Stuttgart
places.note: Steep Keuper slopes above the Neckar within the city, with the Mönchberg and Herzogenberg sites among them.

places.name: Remstal
places.note: The Rems valley east of Stuttgart, with Stetten's Pulvermächer and other Keuper sites giving some of the region's finest Riesling.

places.name: Württembergisch Unterland
places.note: The largest Bereich, the lower land around Heilbronn and the middle Neckar, on Keuper and Muschelkalk. It holds the terraced river sites, the great cooperatives and the villages that make most of the region's Trollinger and Lemberger.

places.name: Heilbronn
places.note: The wine town of the north with large cooperative cellars and the Wartberg vineyard above it; Neckar terraces run south from here.

places.name: Besigheim, Hessigheim and Mundelsheim
places.note: The middle Neckar's terraced Muschelkalk sites behind dry stone walls, the Hessigheimer Felsengärten the most dramatic, worked by hand for Trollinger, Lemberger and Riesling.

places.name: Weinsberg
places.note: Home of the state viticultural school founded in 1868, the oldest in Germany, which bred Kerner and Dornfelder and keeps its own estate on the Schemelsberg.

places.name: Schwaigern and Bönnigheim
places.note: Keuper villages of the Heilbronn and Zabergäu country whose estates built Lemberger's modern reputation.

places.name: Brackenheim
places.note: The Zabergäu town often called Germany's largest red wine commune, on Keuper, with Trollinger and Lemberger throughout.

places.name: Kocher-Jagst-Tauber
places.note: The small northern Bereich on Muschelkalk along three rivers, cooler, with more white grapes than the rest of the region, and close in style to neighbouring Tauberfranken.

places.name: Oberer Neckar
places.note: A tiny Bereich of scattered vineyards up the Neckar around Rottenburg and Tübingen, mostly for local consumption.

places.name: Württembergischer Bodensee and Bayerischer Bodensee
places.note: Two detached Bereiche on the shores of Lake Constance; the Bavarian one, around Lindau, lies in Bavaria yet belongs to the Württemberg region, with Müller-Thurgau and Spätburgunder on moraine.

producers.name: Aldinger

producers.name: Schnaitmann
producers.why: Fellbach grower who made the case for serious Spätburgunder and Lemberger from Keuper.

producers.name: Graf Neipperg
producers.why: The Schwaigern house most associated with Lemberger, which it has championed for generations.

producers.name: Dautel
producers.why: Bönnigheim estate known for barrel aged Lemberger and Spätburgunder of real polish.

producers.name: Graf Adelmann
producers.why: The Kleinbottwar estate at Burg Schaubeck, a long standing name for Lemberger and Samtrot.

producers.name: Wöhrwag
producers.why: Untertürkheim estate working steep Stuttgart slopes for Riesling and Lemberger.

producers.name: Herzog von Württemberg
producers.why: The ducal estate at Ludwigsburg, a historic name with holdings across the region.

producers.name: Karl Haidle
producers.why: Remstal estate whose Stetten Pulvermächer Riesling shows the valley's white side.

producers.name: Staatsweingut Weinsberg

terroir.climate: Continental, with cold winters, warm summers and a growing season sheltered by the Swabian hills from the worst of the west. The Neckar valley and its side valleys trap warmth, which is what lets late ripening Trollinger and Lemberger succeed this far north, while low ground near the rivers suffers spring and autumn frost. Rainfall is moderate and the summers can be dry.
terroir.soils: Keuper dominates: gypsum bearing marls and coloured clays of the Triassic that give the Remstal, the Stuttgart slopes and the Heilbronn country their sturdy reds. Muschelkalk shell limestone surfaces along the middle Neckar at Besigheim, Hessigheim and Mundelsheim and in the Tauber country to the north. Loess and loam cover the gentler ground, and the Bodensee vineyards sit on glacial moraine.
terroir.topography: The Neckar cuts a winding valley with steep south facing flanks that were terraced centuries ago behind dry stone walls, the Steillagen that are the region's pride and its labour problem. Away from the river the vineyards spread over rolling Keuper hills between orchards and towns, often inside the suburbs of Stuttgart itself. Two small outposts sit far to the south on the shores of Lake Constance.
terroir.water: The Neckar is the spine, joined by the Rems, the Enz, the Kocher and the Jagst, with the Tauber marking the north. The river's bends make the terraced sites and moderate the frost on their slopes. Lake Constance, the Bodensee, moderates the two detached southern Bereiche and gives them light and a long autumn.

traps: Schwarzriesling is Pinot Meunier and has nothing to do with Riesling.
Trollinger is Schiava, not a Pinot and not a crossing; it needs the warmest ground because it ripens so late.
Schillerwein is not a blend of finished wines and not a rosé from one grape; it is a Rotling, co-fermented.
Weissherbst is the single variety rosé; do not confuse it with Schillerwein.
Dornfelder is a Weinsberg crossing from Württemberg, though the Pfalz and Rheinhessen grow most of it.
Württemberg's Riesling is dry and fuller than the Mosel's; do not read the region as sweet.
The Bayerischer Bodensee is in Bavaria but is a Bereich of Württemberg, not of Franken.

wines.note: Pale ruby, light bodied, with strawberry and a soft, often slightly sweet finish; serve it cool in a Viertele, the local quarter litre, with Maultaschen or a sausage salad.
The classic local blend, Trollinger's lightness given a little colour and grip by Lemberger; easy, cheerful and made for the Besen, the seasonal grower's tavern.
Dark cherry, black pepper, firm tannin and bright acidity, from unoaked village wine to barrique aged single site GG; Württemberg's answer to a serious red, good with game and roast beef.
A Rotling: red and white grapes fermented together, pale, fresh and local, protected to Württemberg at Qualitätswein level and above.
Dry, firm and fuller than the Mosel's, from Keuper and limestone terraces; the white that accompanies the region's reds at table.
Pinot Meunier as a still red: pale, soft, red fruited and gentle, rarely seen outside the region.
Pinot Noir from the best slopes, fragrant and structured in the modern style, increasingly a Grosses Gewächs grape here.
